mcq.q: When is a plain parallel workflow better than a coordinator agent?
options: When the decomposition can be written in code
Never; a coordinator agent is always more flexible
When the tasks are open-ended and the plan unknown
When each subtask needs different tools
mcq.why: If you know the split, code is cheaper and more predictable.
distractors: When the plan is known, code is cheaper and more predictable.
Open-ended tasks are where a coordinator can help.
Different tools can still run in a fixed workflow.

mcq.q: Choose all the conditions under which multiple agents help.
options: The subtasks are tightly coupled and short
The task needs more material than fits in one context
Subtasks need different tools or permissions
An independent reviewer with fresh context is useful
mcq.why: Breadth, separable expertise, independent verification and organisational boundaries justify multiple agents.
distractors: Tightly coupled, short tasks are where multiple agents do not help.

mcq.q: Published reports on research agents describe multi-agent systems using how many tokens compared with single-agent chat?
options: A fixed 10% more than single-agent chat
About the same number of tokens
Several times to an order of magnitude more
About half, since workers share the work
mcq.why: Parallel workers each read and summarise, so token use grows a lot.
distractors: Coordination and parallel reading add many tokens.
Splitting work does not reduce total tokens.

mcq.q: Why does a single agent fail the chapter's Q3 complaints example?
options: It cannot call tools at all in that design
Its context would fill on the first of three sources
It is slower to start than a team of agents
It is not allowed to read support tickets
mcq.why: Breadth exceeds one context, so workers read parts and return condensed findings.
distractors: Start-up time is not the problem.
Access is not the stated problem.

mcq.q: Mixing billing tools and identity tools in one agent's prompt tends to…
options: Reduce the cost of each run
Improve accuracy on both tasks
Degrade tool selection
Have no effect on behaviour
mcq.why: Separable tools and permissions are a reason to split agents.
distractors: Mixing tools does not cut cost.

mcq.q: Why does independent verification need a separate reviewer?
options: Two agents always agree on the truth
The reviewer is always a bigger model
It halves the cost of the work
A fresh context sees what the producer missed
mcq.why: A reviewer that shares the producer's context shares its blind spots.

mcq.q: Three agents agree on an answer, but all read the same outdated document. What does the agreement show?
options: Little: they share the same wrong source
That the answer is certainly correct
That the document must be current
That no further verification is needed
mcq.why: Agreement between agents with the same evidence is not independent validation.
distractors: Shared sources call for more checks.

mcq.q: Each worker in the example returns a 300-word summary with evidence IDs. Why not return raw records?
options: Raw records cannot be sent between agents
Summaries are cheaper to store in a database
To protect the coordinator's context and stay traceable
Evidence IDs are optional in any design
mcq.why: Condensed findings with evidence let the coordinator synthesise without overflowing.

mcq.q: Which is an organisational reason for multiple agents?
options: The team simply prefers to build more agents
The task has only one short step
Agents owned by different teams or vendors
One model is too cheap to be trusted
mcq.why: Ownership boundaries can require separate agents.
distractors: Cost is not an organisational reason.

mcq.q: A task is “summarise each of these 20 contracts, then compare”. What should you build?
options: A single agent with 20 contract tools
A coordinator agent that discovers the plan
A supervisor hierarchy over the workers
Parallel LLM calls in code, then a compare call
mcq.why: If the decomposition can be written in code, do that; it is cheaper and more predictable.
distractors: The plan is known; code can run it.

mcq.q: A single agent costs $0.15 per task and succeeds 70% of the time. A multi-agent design costs $1.20 and succeeds 85%. What is the cost per successful task for each?
options: About $0.11 single, about $1.02 multi
About $0.15 single, about $1.20 multi
About $0.21 single, about $1.41 multi
About $0.50 single, about $8.00 multi
mcq.why: 0.15 ÷ 0.70 ≈ $0.21; 1.20 ÷ 0.85 ≈ $1.41. The multi-agent design costs over 6× more per success.
distractors: That multiplies by the success rate instead of dividing.
That is cost per task, ignoring failures.
That divides by the failure rate.

mcq.q: A team proposes a coordinator and three worker agents to translate one two-page letter into French. What does the chapter suggest?
options: An evaluator loop that critiques until the letter is perfect
A single call: the task is short and not separable
A supervisor hierarchy, so a manager can check each worker
A coordinator and workers, so each worker translates a paragraph
mcq.why: Multiple agents do not help short or coupled tasks, and they add cost.
distractors: Hierarchies multiply cost for a tiny task.
The paragraphs depend on each other for tone and terms.

interview.q: When do multiple agents help, and when do they not?
covers: not for coupled or short tasks
interview.followUp: Give an example where a single agent beat a team in your experience or reading.

interview.q: What does a multi-agent design cost compared with a single agent?
covers: several to many times the tokens

interview.q: Why is agreement between agents not proof of correctness?
interview.followUp: How would you get independent evidence?

interview.q: A team wants a coordinator agent for a report whose steps are always the same. What do you suggest?
covers: keep agents for parts that vary
interview.followUp: What would change your mind?

interview.q: How would you decide whether to split one agent into a billing agent and an account agent?
interview.followUp: How would you measure tool-selection errors?

interview.q: Your multi-agent research system costs 8× a single agent. How do you decide if it is worth it?
covers: quality gain on the same suite
use it only where it wins
interview.followUp: Where would you use it, and where not?

interview.q: {company} wants an agent system that plans multi-city trips. Single agent, workflow or several agents? Justify.
interview.followUp: Where would you put human confirmation?

interview.q: Design a system that summarises complaints across tickets, sales notes and app reviews, each with different access rules.
interview.followUp: How do you stop one worker's access rules leaking into the synthesis?

mcq.q: Each of 6 sequential steps is 95% reliable. End to end is about…
mcq.why: 0.95⁶ ≈ 0.74; errors compound along the chain.
distractors: 95% is one step; the chain multiplies six of them.
A chain is less reliable than one step, not more.

mcq.q: Two workers report different facts. How should the coordinator resolve it?
options: Pick the worker whose answer sounds more confident
Use evidence, recency, authority or a check; surface the rest
Pick whichever result was returned to it first
Average the two facts into a single middle answer
mcq.why: Resolve with rules and evidence; do not average conflicts away.

mcq.q: Each of 10 sequential steps is 90% reliable. What is end-to-end reliability?
options: About 35%
About 10%
About 65%
About 90%

mcq.q: Each of 6 steps is 95% reliable, and a verifier catches 50% of each step's errors. What is end-to-end reliability?
options: About 86%
About 50%
About 95%
About 74%

mcq.q: How does one worker's hallucination become a bigger problem?
options: It is always caught during the synthesis step
It becomes the coordinator's premise and headline
It only affects that one worker's own output
It reduces the run's token cost slightly
mcq.why: Errors propagate through the chain; evidence requirements break it.
distractors: Synthesis tends to build on it.

mcq.q: Choose all the defences against runaway loops.
options: Telling the evaluator to approve only perfect work
A run-level budget
Global step, depth and spawn limits
A maximum number of critique rounds
mcq.why: Hard limits stop loops; “perfect” criteria cause them.
distractors: That is how the chapter's 14-round loop happened.

mcq.q: In the chapter's runaway critique example, what fixed it?
options: Removing the producer agent from the loop
A concrete rubric, 2 rounds max, then ship with notes
Raising the budget available for each report
A stronger, more capable evaluator model
mcq.why: Concrete criteria and a round limit end the loop.
distractors: The work still had to be done.
A stronger critic can still never approve.

mcq.q: When can coordination overhead exceed the useful work?
options: Only with one worker
Never
On small tasks
Only on very large tasks
mcq.why: Briefs, summaries and synthesis cost tokens whatever the task size.
distractors: One worker has the least overhead.

mcq.q: A 2024 policy and a 2026 amendment conflict. Which rule should decide?
options: The first worker to finish
The more articulate answer
Authority and effective date
The longer document
mcq.why: Source authority and recency rules resolve the conflict.

mcq.q: Agents send “please clarify” to each other repeatedly. Which control detects this?
options: Loop detection on repeated messages
A faster model for both agents
More workers to share the load
A larger context window for each
mcq.why: Repeated messages are a loop signal.
distractors: Speed does not stop a loop.
More agents can add more loops.

mcq.q: A chain has 4 sequential steps, each 90% reliable. A verifier catches and corrects 80% of each step's errors. What is the end-to-end reliability?
options: About 72%, which is 0.9⁴ plus the verifier's 80% share
About 80%, the verifier's catch rate sets the ceiling
About 98%, since the verifier fixes most errors
About 92%, against about 66% without the verifier
distractors: The verifier acts on each step's errors, not once at the end.
The ceiling comes from compounding per step.
That is one step; the chain has four.

interview.q: How should a coordinator resolve conflicting worker outputs?
interview.followUp: When should a conflict reach the user unresolved?

interview.q: Why does reliability compound across steps, and what breaks the chain?
interview.followUp: Compute 0.95^6.

interview.q: What causes runaway loops in multi-agent systems?
interview.followUp: Which limit catches the most loops in practice?

interview.q: An evaluator agent rejected a report 14 times. How do you fix the system?
covers: ship with notes for a human
interview.followUp: What goes into the rubric?

interview.q: Where would you add verification in a six-step chain, given a fixed budget?
covers: steps with highest error or impact
interview.followUp: What does the verifier cost, and how do you justify it?

interview.q: A false fact from one worker appeared in an executive report. Trace and prevent it.
interview.followUp: How would you test that the fix works?

interview.q: Two of {company}'s workers return different fares for the same route. Design the resolution rule and what the traveller sees.
covers: tell the traveller the price changed
interview.followUp: What if the live check fails?

interview.q: Design run-level guards for a platform where agents can spawn other agents.

mcq.q: A worker with broad credentials executes a lower-trust user's request. This is…
options: least privilege
a confused deputy
a race condition
prompt caching
mcq.why: Pass the user's identity and narrow scopes at each hop instead.
distractors: Least privilege is the fix, not the problem.

mcq.q: When agent A asks agent B to act, whose permissions should apply by default?
options: The broadest permissions available
Agent A's own permissions
The user's, narrowed at each hop
Agent B's service account
mcq.why: Narrowing the user's rights at each hop prevents escalation.
distractors: A service account may exceed the user's rights.

mcq.q: What does OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) do at each hop?
options: Swaps it for one with narrower audience and scopes
Removes the user's identity from the token
Copies the incoming token unchanged
Adds the agent's own admin scopes
mcq.why: Each hop can only reduce permissions; tokens are short-lived.
distractors: Then it would be valid everywhere.

mcq.q: A coordinator tells its worker agents whom they act for by passing a plain user_id string. A security review flags this. Why?
options: Tokens are faster to process than strings
User IDs are not unique across systems
Any agent could forge a plain ID
Strings are too long to pass between agents
mcq.why: A signed token proves who the user is; a string does not.

mcq.q: Where should the final access decision be made?
options: By the coordinator agent, for its workers
By the model, from the request
At the resource, using both identities
By the worker that holds the token
mcq.why: Agents never decide access for themselves.

mcq.q: What does an agent's own workload identity (e.g. SPIFFE/mTLS) add?
options: It shows which agent acted for which user
It encrypts the prompts sent to the model
It replaces the user's identity in calls
It grants the agent admin rights
mcq.why: Both identities appear: “agent B acting for Alice, requested by agent A”.

mcq.q: In the chapter's figure, the finance API checks…
options: Only the worker's allowed scopes
Whatever the model asks it to do
Alice's rights ∩ the worker's scopes
Only Alice's own rights
mcq.why: The intersection means writes are refused even if the model asks.

mcq.q: An intern asks a reporting agent with a service account for HR salary data. With on-behalf-of tokens, what happens?
options: The agent returns the salary data
The agent asks HR for it by email
The request is queued until later
The HR API sees the intern and denies it
mcq.why: The resource checks the real requester, so the confused deputy is avoided.

mcq.q: Can the coordinator request scopes Alice does not have?
options: No: each hop can only narrow
Yes, if the model asks for them
Only for read-only scopes
Yes, for internal APIs only
mcq.why: Token exchange enforces narrowing.

mcq.q: What should the audit trail record for a delegated action?
options: Only the final agent that acted
Only the user who started it
Nothing; the tokens are enough
The full chain: user, agents, resource
mcq.why: Investigators need to see which agent acted and for whom (16.7).
distractors: Tokens expire and are not records.

mcq.q: Alice's token allows invoices.read. The coordinator asks the token service for a finance-api token with invoices.write, on Alice's behalf. What happens?
options: It succeeds if the model says the write is needed
It succeeds for internal APIs such as finance-api
It succeeds, since the coordinator is a trusted service
The exchange is refused: a hop cannot add scopes Alice lacks
mcq.why: Token exchange only narrows audience and scopes.
distractors: Internal APIs follow the same rule.
Trust in the agent does not widen Alice's rights.

mcq.q: After an incident, logs show a record was changed by “svc-agents”, a service account shared by all agents. Investigators cannot tell which agent acted, or for whom. What was missing?
options: Per-agent identities and the delegation chain in the audit trail
A larger log retention period for the service account
More detailed system prompts for each of the agents
A shorter-lived token for the shared service account
mcq.why: Each agent needs its own identity, and logs must record user ← agent ← agent.
distractors: Longer retention keeps the same missing detail.
Expiry does not identify the agent.

interview.followUp: How do you avoid breaking agents during the migration?

interview.followUp: How would you handle a worker that runs on a schedule with no user?

interview.q: Design authorisation for agents that call each other across teams.
interview.followUp: How do you revoke an agent's access quickly across teams?

mcq.q: Which pattern lets the active agent transfer the conversation to another agent?
options: Coordinator–worker
Evaluator–optimiser
Routing
Handoff
mcq.why: In a handoff, control of the conversation moves to the next agent.
distractors: The coordinator keeps control and delegates subtasks.
Routing sends a request to one specialist before work starts.

mcq.q: What is the main risk of routing?
options: Endless critique loops between agents
Context too large for a single model
Misrouting; it needs an “other” path
Deep hierarchies that add latency
mcq.why: A router can send a request to the wrong specialist; an “other” path catches unknown types.

mcq.q: What should a handoff pass to the next agent?
options: A structured summary: ID, issue, evidence, what was said
Nothing; the next agent starts afresh with the customer
The full transcript plus every tool the first agent had
Only the customer's name and email address
mcq.why: A summary keeps context without overloading or over-sharing; the next agent gets only its own tools.
distractors: Too much context and too much access.

mcq.q: When does the evaluator–optimiser pattern work well?
options: For real-time routing
When no criteria exist
When the evaluator is the same model with the same context
When there are clear quality criteria for drafts
mcq.why: Without clear criteria, the loop may never end; the same model and context share blind spots.
distractors: That is how endless loops start.

mcq.q: What is the main risk of a supervisor hierarchy?
options: No one can override the workers
It has no central point of control
It cannot replan once started
Deep hierarchies multiply cost and latency
mcq.why: Each management layer adds calls.

mcq.q: Two agents keep handing a customer back and forth. What is this called and what limits it?
options: A saga; add compensating actions
Caching; clear the cache between agents
Ping-pong; cap handoffs and escalate
Routing; add more routes to choose from
mcq.why: Handoff ping-pong is a known risk; cap handoffs and send to a person.
distractors: More routes do not stop bouncing.

mcq.q: Which pattern fits a breadth-first task with separable parts?
options: Coordinator–worker
Handoff
Routing
Evaluator–optimiser
mcq.why: The coordinator decomposes, delegates and synthesises.

mcq.q: A general support agent hands a disputed-charge case to the billing agent. Which tools should the billing agent be given?
options: No tools
Every tool the general agent had
Only billing tools
Admin tools
mcq.why: Least privilege applies to each agent after a handoff.
distractors: It needs billing tools to act.

mcq.q: Who should own completion of a task in a multi-agent design?
options: Every agent equally
Whoever finishes last
No one; agents agree among themselves
One clearly named agent or component
mcq.why: Unclear ownership leads each agent to assume another will finish.

mcq.q: A coordinator in Harbor's design is plain code. Which pattern is that closest to?
options: Handoff between two support agents
Coordinator–worker, coordinated by code
Evaluator–optimiser with a critic
Supervisor hierarchy with a manager
mcq.why: The coordinator role can be code rather than a model when the plan is fixed.

mcq.q: Support requests are password resets, invoice questions or shipping problems, each needing different tools; about 5% are something else. Which pattern fits?
options: A coordinator that sends each request to all three agents
An evaluator–optimiser loop on every incoming request
A supervisor hierarchy with a manager over three teams
Routing to one specialist each, with an “other” path
mcq.why: Distinct request types with distinct tools suit routing; misrouting needs an “other” path.
distractors: Fan-out wastes work when one specialist fits.
There is no draft to critique.
Hierarchy adds cost without a long task to oversee.

mcq.q: A team drafts marketing emails that must pass a 10-point brand checklist. Which pattern fits, and what must it include?
options: Handoff, passing the email between departments
Routing, with one agent per section of the email
Evaluator–optimiser, with a concrete checklist and a cap on rounds
Coordinator–worker, with one worker per checklist item
mcq.why: Clear criteria suit a critic loop; the cap stops endless revision.
distractors: Routing picks one specialist; it does not revise drafts.
Ten workers for one email multiplies cost.

interview.followUp: What does the customer see when you escalate?

interview.followUp: What would the customer see at each step?

interview.q: Design a support system where several departments each own an agent.
interview.followUp: Who owns a request that touches two departments?

mcq.q: What should a task brief include?
options: Objective, constraints, tools, budget, schema
The coordinator's full context and history
Only the objective of the task, nothing more
The expected final answer to check against
mcq.why: A clear brief keeps workers focused and outputs combinable.
distractors: Workers need only what their task needs.

mcq.q: Six subtasks take 10, 20, 30, 10, 20 and 30 seconds. Ignoring overhead, how long does sequential execution take, and how long with all six in parallel?
options: 120 s both ways
60 s sequential; 20 s parallel
120 s sequential; 30 s parallel
30 s sequential; 120 s parallel
mcq.why: Sequential is the sum (120 s); unlimited parallel waits for the slowest (30 s).

mcq.q: Parallel execution cuts wall-clock time. What happens to total token cost?
options: It halves
It drops to zero for workers
It stays the same or rises
It falls in proportion to parallelism
mcq.why: The same work is done, plus coordination overhead.

mcq.q: Why set a concurrency limit?
options: To protect rate limits and budgets
To make workers smarter
To reduce the number of subtasks
To avoid synthesis
mcq.why: Unbounded parallel calls can hit provider rate limits and spend fast.

mcq.q: A coordinator delegates “research the market” to three workers. What is the likely result?
options: A faster, cheaper run
Three complementary reports
An error from the framework
Overlapping, unfocused work
mcq.why: Vague delegation produces vague, overlapping outputs.

mcq.q: Synthesis must wait for the slowest worker unless…
options: You set a deadline and use what returned
You switch to a bigger model
You add more workers to the run
You remove the output schema
mcq.why: A deadline bounds latency; missing parts are marked.
distractors: The schema is not the delay.

mcq.q: Which describes good decomposition?
options: Subtasks that each need the others' full detail to proceed
As many subtasks as possible, however small each one is
One subtask for every tool the agents have available
Independent subtasks with objective, scope, format and stopping rule
mcq.why: Independence enables parallelism; clarity prevents overlap.

mcq.q: What should synthesis keep so the final result is traceable?
options: The workers' token counts
Only the final text
Each worker's full transcript
Evidence links from the workers
mcq.why: Evidence links let reviewers check each claim.
distractors: Transcripts are too large for synthesis.

mcq.q: Workers each return 5,000-token raw dumps to a coordinator with a 32,000-token window and an 8,000-token system prompt and policy. How many workers fit before the window is full?
options: Unlimited
mcq.why: 32,000 − 8,000 = 24,000 tokens left; 24,000 / 5,000 = 4.8, so 4 full results fit. Condensed findings avoid this limit.
distractors: That ignores the 8,000 tokens already used.

mcq.q: What context should a worker receive?
options: Everything the coordinator knows
Only what its subtask needs
The other workers' results
Nothing but the objective
mcq.why: Minimal context reduces cost and keeps data access least-privilege.
distractors: They are not needed and add noise.
Too little to do the task.

mcq.q: Six subtasks take 10, 20, 30, 15, 25 and 40 seconds. They run in parallel with a limit of 6, then synthesis takes 10 s. Roughly what is the wall-clock time?
options: About 33 s: the average task plus synthesis
About 50 s: the slowest worker plus synthesis
About 150 s: the sum of all tasks plus synthesis
About 40 s: synthesis runs alongside the workers
mcq.why: All six run at once, so the wait is the 40 s worker, then 10 s of synthesis.
distractors: Synthesis waits for the slowest worker, not the average.

mcq.q: What is a blackboard in multi-agent design?
options: A private context for each agent
An approval screen for humans
A shared store agents read and write
A logging system for traces
mcq.why: Shared state is easy to coordinate but risks conflicts and leakage.
distractors: Logs are not shared working state.

mcq.q: Choose all the risks of shared state.
options: Conflicting writes
Permission leakage
Context pollution (everyone sees everything)
Agents cannot communicate
mcq.why: Shared stores spread data and conflicts; communication is easy, not impossible.

mcq.q: What does isolated state require?
options: Explicit, well-designed messages
A shared free-text scratchpad
One model for every agent
No schemas for messages
mcq.why: Agents communicate only through messages, so contracts matter.

mcq.q: Which fields belong in a result contract, per the chapter?
options: The worker's full chain of thought
The worker's API keys and tokens
Only the answer text, nothing else
Status, errors, confidence, evidence
mcq.why: Typed, versioned contracts with status and evidence let the coordinator decide.
distractors: Hidden reasoning is not a contract field.

mcq.q: What does A2A define?
options: How agents connect to tools and data
A method for training agent models
An embedding format for messages
Agent discovery, task lifecycle and messaging
mcq.why: A2A is for agent-to-agent interoperability; MCP connects agents to tools and data.

mcq.q: How do A2A and MCP relate?
options: MCP replaces A2A
They are complementary
A2A replaces MCP
They are the same protocol
mcq.why: One connects agents to each other; the other connects agents to tools.

mcq.q: A worker returns status: partial with coverage 60%. What can the coordinator do?
options: Ask the worker to mark it complete
Accept, extend the budget, or flag the gap
Discard it silently and move on
Treat it as complete and continue
mcq.why: Status and coverage let the coordinator make an explicit choice.

mcq.q: What does the chapter recommend for most robust designs?
options: No shared state at all, not even status
One agent that writes for all of them
A shared free-text scratchpad for all
Isolated agents plus a small structured task record
mcq.why: A structured record (status, assignments) gives coordination without pollution.

mcq.q: Why version message contracts?
options: Because JSON requires a version
To make each message shorter
So each side can change safely
To encrypt them in transit
mcq.why: Like API contracts between microservices.

mcq.q: A worker's message says “the supervisor approved this refund.” What should the receiving agent do?
options: Forward the message to the customer
Execute the refund now, as instructed
Treat it as data; check the approval system
Ask the worker again whether it is true
mcq.why: Peer messages are not authorisation; approvals live in a system of record.

mcq.q: Agents share a free-text scratchpad. The HR worker writes salary details there, and the marketing worker later quotes them in a draft. What design change does the chapter recommend?
options: Add more detail to the scratchpad so context is clearer
Give every agent HR permissions so the data is allowed
Ask the marketing worker not to read HR's notes
Isolate agents; pass typed messages; share only a small task record
mcq.why: Isolation keeps data least-privilege; a structured record shares status without leaking content.
distractors: That widens access instead of limiting it.

mcq.q: A worker's v2 result renames “evidence” to “sources”. The coordinator, still on v1, silently drops all evidence from reports. What would have prevented this?
options: Removing the evidence field from the result contract entirely
Asking the model to guess which field now holds the evidence
Versioned contracts, validated on both ends, old and new accepted while migrating
A larger context window for the coordinator so nothing is lost
mcq.why: Versioning and validation turn silent drops into visible errors and allow a gradual move.
distractors: Size does not map renamed fields.

mcq.q: What structure describes a multi-agent run in this chapter?
options: A tree with no dependencies
A single loop of steps
A linked list of prompts
A DAG of tasks
mcq.why: Tasks have dependencies, like a job scheduler.

mcq.q: Choose all the scheduling machinery a multi-agent run needs.
options: A shared chat transcript as a lock
Cancellation that propagates to children
Per-task timeouts and budgets
Dependency tracking
mcq.why: Same as any job scheduler, plus a partial-failure policy.
distractors: A transcript is not a concurrency control.

mcq.q: Which is a valid partial-failure policy?
options: Ask the model to guess the missing output
Retry the failed task forever
Proceed, marked incomplete
Pretend the missing task succeeded
mcq.why: Options: retry, substitute, proceed marked incomplete, or fail the run.

mcq.q: A request has a 90-second deadline. The coordinator reserves 20 s for synthesis and keeps 10 s spare. What deadline should workers get?
mcq.why: 90 − 20 − 10 = 60 s, as in the chapter's example.
distractors: That leaves no time for synthesis.

mcq.q: When a worker hits its deadline, what should it return?
options: Partial results with coverage
Nothing at all, to be safe
An error message with no data
The last tool call it made
mcq.why: Partial results degrade gracefully (15.6).
distractors: A tool call is not a result.

mcq.q: A user cancels mid-run. What must cancellation do?
options: Only hide the run from the user's screen
Wait for all running workers to finish
Stop running children and their tool calls
Cancel only the coordinator, not workers
mcq.why: Cancelled work must stop spending and acting.

mcq.q: Does promise-style parallel code (e.g. Promise.all) give durable scheduling?
options: Only when it runs on a server
No: it survives no restarts
Yes, always, in any runtime
Yes, if every promise is awaited
mcq.why: In-process concurrency is not durable and does not undo actions.
distractors: Location does not make it durable.

mcq.q: Worker B times out after finishing its tool calls. The run proceeded and the answer was finalised. B's result arrives later. What should happen?
options: Keep the answer; log it or use it later
Restart the whole run from scratch
Overwrite the answer that was given
Merge it in silently afterwards
mcq.why: A late result must not alter a finalised answer without a new, explicit step.

mcq.q: Worker deadlines should be ___ than the deadline of the request that spawned them.
options: Tighter
Looser
The same
Unrelated
mcq.why: Deadlines flow down, each hop tighter, leaving time for later steps.
distractors: No time would remain for synthesis.
They must be derived from the parent.

mcq.q: Synthesis needs workers A, B and C. Worker C errors, the policy retries it once, and the retry succeeds. What happens next?
options: Synthesis runs with all three
All three workers are run again
The run fails because C errored
Synthesis runs without C, incomplete
mcq.why: A successful retry satisfies the dependency; nothing is missing.

mcq.q: Synthesis needs workers A, B and C. B times out at its deadline, and the policy is to proceed with partial results. What should the final report do?
options: Use A and C and leave B's area out without comment
Use A and C, and mark B's area as incomplete
Fail the whole run, since one worker timed out
Ask the model to fill in B's area from its own knowledge
mcq.why: Proceeding with partial results means saying clearly what is missing.
distractors: That is a different policy from the one chosen.

mcq.q: What should a multi-agent design be compared against?
options: A deliberately weak baseline that is easy to beat
A strong single agent and a parallel workflow, same suite
Last year's model on a different test set
Nothing, since it is clearly the better design
mcq.why: It must beat the strongest simple alternative at acceptable cost.

mcq.q: What does pass^3 measure?
options: Success on the third attempt
Three times the success rate
Tasks that succeed in all three runs
Success when three agents run
mcq.why: It measures reliability over repeated runs.
distractors: It is about runs, not agents.

mcq.q: In the chapter's illustrative table, why does the parallel workflow ship?
options: Most of the gain; the team adds 3 points for ~4× cost
It has the lowest latency because it is simpler
It has the highest task success of all
It is the cheapest of the designs
mcq.why: 78% vs 81% success, but $0.21 vs $0.88 per successful task and 31 s vs 112 s p95.

mcq.q: A design costs $0.30 per task and succeeds on 60% of tasks. What is its cost per successful task?
What is an ablation in this context?
options: Adding more agents to the design
Removing a part to see if quality drops
Training a model on the outputs
Running the same design twice
mcq.why: For example, remove the evaluator or merge two workers.

mcq.q: In the chapter's ablation example, removing the critic changed success from 81% to 80%. What did the team do?
options: Added a second critic everywhere
Kept it only for high-stakes reports
Kept the critic for every report
Removed every agent in the design
mcq.why: A drop within noise did not justify 30% more cost and 35% more latency.
distractors: The data did not justify it.

mcq.q: Choose all the component metrics the chapter suggests.
options: Routing accuracy
Synthesis faithfulness to worker outputs
Number of agents in the design
Worker success per subtask
mcq.why: Also how often conflicts are surfaced correctly.
distractors: Agent count is not a quality metric.

mcq.q: Why re-run the comparison when models improve?
options: Older results are always wrong
Multi-agent designs get cheaper automatically
Benchmarks expire
A stronger single agent may close the gap
mcq.why: Model upgrades change the trade-off.
distractors: They are not wrong, just possibly outdated.

mcq.q: On a CPU laptop with one Ollama instance, why are wall-clock gains from parallel workers small?
options: Calls queue unless OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL allows more
CPUs cannot run language models at all
Ollama does not support agents or tools
Parallel code is not allowed in Python scripts
mcq.why: The quality and token comparison is still valid.

mcq.q: Why is comparing an agent team with a deliberately weak single-agent baseline a problem?
options: It makes pass^k impossible to compute
Weak baselines are cheaper to run
It inflates the apparent gain of the team design
Single agents cannot be evaluated
mcq.why: The design must beat the strongest simple alternative, not a straw man.
distractors: Cost is not the issue; the comparison is misleading.
They can, on the same suite.
